name: Mesopotamia
summary: Mesopotamia's civilizations rose and fell in succession along the Tigris and Euphrates: Sumerian city-states gave way to Sargon's Akkadian Empire, then the Sumerian revival under the Third Dynasty of Ur, Hammurabi's Babylon, the Neo-Assyrian Empire centered on Nineveh, and finally the Neo-Babylonian Empire, which fell to Cyrus the Great of Persia in 539 BC.
imageAttribution: Map by Goran tek-en, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of ancient Mesopotamia along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

events.title: Cuneiform Emerges at Uruk
events.body: The world's earliest writing system develops from clay tokens used to record grain and livestock at the city of Uruk, becoming the first script for recording language and law.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A monumental Achaemenid-era cuneiform inscription of Xerxes I, carved into the cliff at Van in eastern Turkey.

events.title: Sargon Founds the Akkadian Empire
events.body: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian city-states and unites them under a single ruler, creating what many historians consider the world's first empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by ALFGRN, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Sargon of Akkad depicted on his victory stele.

events.title: Ur-Nammu Founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
events.body: After centuries of Akkadian and Gutian rule, Ur-Nammu reunites southern Mesopotamia under the city of Ur and issues the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest law code known to survive.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Sémhur and Zunkir, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Third Dynasty of Ur's territorial extent under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi.

events.title: Hammurabi's Code Carved in Stone
events.body: Babylon's king publishes 282 laws on a black diorite stele, one of the earliest surviving law codes governing an entire society.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mbzt, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The front face of the Code of Hammurabi stele, now in the Louvre.

events.title: Ashurbanipal Builds the Library at Nineveh
events.body: Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembles a vast collection of cuneiform tablets at his capital, creating the ancient world's most systematic library and preserving countless Mesopotamian texts for posterity.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by KeyolTranslater, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief of King Ashurbanipal hunting lions, from his palace at Nineveh.

events.title: Nineveh Falls
events.body: A coalition of Babylonians and Medes storms the Assyrian capital, ending the Neo-Assyrian Empire's centuries of dominance over the Near East.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Mu-tamajo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: John Martin's 1829 painting The Fall of Nineveh.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II Conquers Jerusalem
events.body: After a lengthy siege, Babylonian forces breach Jerusalem's walls, destroy Solomon's Temple, and deport much of the population -- the start of the Babylonian captivity that Cyrus will later end.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Etemenanki, the great ziggurat of Babylon rebuilt under Nebuchadnezzar II.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.body: Cyrus of Persia captures Babylon without a major battle, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire and folding Mesopotamia into the Achaemenid Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Mezzotint by J. Martin (1831), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons / Wellcome Collection
events.imageDescription: J. Martin's 1831 mezzotint depicting Cyrus the Great's conquest of Babylon.

name: Egypt
summary: Ancient Egypt's civilization ran from Narmer's unification of Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BC through the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms -- each followed by a period of fragmentation and reunification -- to the Late Period's conquest by Persia, then Alexander the Great, and finally the Ptolemaic dynasty, which ended with Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BC.
imageAttribution: Photo by Douwe C. van der Zee, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A modern photograph of the Pyramid of Khufu at Giza, the last surviving Wonder of the Ancient World.

events.title: Narmer Unites Upper and Lower Egypt
events.body: King Narmer conquers or absorbs Lower Egypt, uniting the Nile valley under a single ruler for the first time and founding the line of pharaohs that will govern Egypt for the next three millennia.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Narmer Palette, a ceremonial carved slate commemorating the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.

events.title: Djoser Builds the Step Pyramid at Saqqara
events.body: Pharaoh Djoser's architect Imhotep builds Egypt's first monumental stone structure, a six-tiered pyramid that launches the Old Kingdom's age of pyramid-building.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
events.imageDescription: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, Egypt's first monumental stone structure.

events.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza Is Completed
events.body: Pharaoh Khufu's tomb is finished after roughly two decades of construction, standing as the largest pyramid ever built and the last surviving Ancient Wonder of the World.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Douwe C. van der Zee, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern photograph of the Great Pyramid of Giza, built as Khufu's tomb.

events.title: Mentuhotep II Reunifies Egypt, Begins the Middle Kingdom
events.body: After more than a century of division known as the First Intermediate Period, Mentuhotep II defeats his rivals and reunites Upper and Lower Egypt, founding the Middle Kingdom from his power base at Thebes.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Prof. Mortel, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A statue of Mentuhotep II from his mortuary complex at Deir el-Bahri, now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

events.title: Ahmose I Expels the Hyksos, Begins the New Kingdom
events.body: Ahmose I captures the Hyksos stronghold of Avaris, driving the foreign dynasty out of Egypt and founding the 18th Dynasty, which will carry Egypt to the height of its power and territorial reach.
events.imageAttribution: Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A carved head of Ahmose I, founder of Egypt's 18th Dynasty, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

events.title: Akhenaten Launches Egypt's Religious Revolution
events.body: Pharaoh Akhenaten abandons Egypt's traditional pantheon for the worship of a single sun-disc god, Aten, and builds a new capital at Amarna -- a radical break that his successors will reverse within a generation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5

events.title: The Battle of Kadesh
events.body: Ramesses II leads Egyptian forces against the Hittite army of Muwatalli II in one of history's largest chariot battles; both sides claim victory, and the standoff eventually produces the world's earliest surviving peace treaty.
events.imageAttribution: Photo via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
events.imageDescription: The temple of Abu Simbel, built by Ramesses II, whose reliefs commemorate his campaign at Kadesh.

events.title: Cambyses II Conquers Egypt for Persia
events.body: The Achaemenid king Cambyses II defeats Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium and crowns himself pharaoh, ending Egypt's Late Period independence and folding it into the Persian Empire as a satrapy.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Mossmaps, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the western Achaemenid Empire, including Egypt after Cambyses II's conquest.

events.title: Alexander the Great Conquers Egypt
events.body: Alexander enters Egypt to a welcome as a liberator from Persian rule and is crowned pharaoh at Memphis, ending nearly two centuries of Achaemenid control and setting up the Macedonian Greek Ptolemaic dynasty that follows.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons (detail of the Alexander Mosaic)
events.imageDescription: A detail of the Alexander Mosaic from Pompeii, depicting Alexander the Great in battle.

events.title: Death of Cleopatra VII
events.body: Egypt's last active pharaoh dies by suicide after Rome's conquest of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, ending nearly three millennia of pharaonic rule and making Egypt a province of Rome.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Louis le Grand, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Roman marble bust of Cleopatra VII, dated to around the time of her visit to Rome, now in Berlin's Altes Museum.

name: Indus Valley
summary: Village farming communities along the Indus and its tributaries grow into walled settlements by 3300 BC, and by 2600 BC these coalesce into a network of standardized cities -- Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, and dozens more -- sharing brick sizes, city planning, and a still-undeciphered script. Indus traders reach Mesopotamia by sea, but the great cities lose population and long-distance contact around 1900 BC as regional rivers dry up, and by 1300 BC the last localized successor cultures fade out, centuries before any written record explains why.
imageAttribution: Map by Avantiputra7, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Indus Valley Civilization's extent during its Mature Phase (2600-1900 BC).

events.title: Early Farming Villages Rise at Kot Diji
events.body: Walled settlements at Kot Diji, on the Indus's east bank opposite the future site of Mohenjo-daro, adopt the fortification style and pottery traditions that mark the start of the Early Harappan period.

events.title: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro Rise
events.body: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro emerge as the Indus Valley's twin great cities, their grid-planned streets, standardized baked-brick sizes, and covered drains opening the seven-century Mature Harappan period.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Muhammad Bin Naveed, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Granary and Great Hall on Mound F at the archaeological site of Harappa.

events.title: A Standardized Script Appears on Seals
events.body: Thousands of carved steatite seals carry a symbol system used widely enough across Mature Harappan cities to suggest formal record-keeping, though without any known bilingual text, the script remains undeciphered today.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by PHGCOM, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Indus Valley seal impression showing a five-character Indus script inscription, in the British Museum.

events.title: Trade Networks Reach Mesopotamia
events.body: Sargon of Akkad's inscriptions describe ships arriving from Meluhha, most likely the Indus Valley, carrying carnelian beads, ivory, and timber to Mesopotamian ports in exchange for silver, wool, and grain.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Sémhur (base) and Zunkir (derivative), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Middle East in the second half of the 3rd millennium BC, spanning the Akkadian and Ur III periods.

events.title: The Mature Harappan Cities Begin to Decline
events.body: Population and long-distance trade at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro start to contract as the seven-century Mature Harappan period ends, opening a slower slide into regional fragmentation.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Saqib Qayyum, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro, a large brick-built pool at the center of the city's citadel, likely used for ritual bathing.

events.title: Cemetery H Culture Marks a Late Harappan Shift
events.body: As Mohenjo-daro is abandoned, a new culture identified by cremation burials in painted urns appears at Harappa's "Cemetery H," with settlement pushing eastward and rice farming replacing the old river-trade economy.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Avantiputra7, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Painted pottery urns from Harappa's Cemetery H period, now in the National Museum, New Delhi.

events.title: The Civilization Fades
events.body: A prolonged drying of the region's rivers drains the water supply that sustained Indus cities, and the last Late Harappan successor cultures fade into isolated regional traditions, centuries before any written record explains their end.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Saqib Qayyum, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of a Buddhist stupa built centuries later atop Mohenjo-daro's citadel mound.

name: Greece
summary: Ancient Greece rose from a loose collection of city-states in the Archaic period, through the Classical age's wars with Persia and each other, to Alexander the Great's Macedonian-led conquests that opened the Hellenistic era -- before falling under Roman control after the Achaean War in 146 BC.
imageAttribution: Photo by Phanatic, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The Parthenon, the temple to Athena atop the Acropolis in Athens.

events.title: The First Olympic Games
events.body: City-states across Greece send athletes to Olympia for a festival of competition held in honor of Zeus, beginning a tradition that will continue every four years for over a thousand years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bgabel, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The ruins of the palaestra (wrestling school) at Olympia, site of the ancient Olympic Games.

events.title: Draco's Harsh Laws Are Written Down
events.body: Athens gets its first written law code under the lawgiver Draco, whose penalties are so severe -- reportedly prescribing death for even minor offenses -- that his name gives us the word "draconian."
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by Max Karl Baldamus, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1833 engraved portrait of the Athenian lawgiver Draco.

events.title: Cleisthenes Founds Athenian Democracy
events.body: Cleisthenes reorganizes Athens' constitution around ten new tribes cutting across old aristocratic loyalties, laying the groundwork for direct democratic government by its citizens.
events.imageAttribution: Unknown artist, CC BY, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern bust of Cleisthenes, regarded as the father of Athenian democracy.

events.title: Victory at Marathon
events.body: An outnumbered Athenian army routs the first Persian invasion force on the plain of Marathon, a victory that becomes a defining Athenian legend of citizen-soldiers defending their homeland.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by John Steeple Davis, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An illustration of the Battle of Marathon.

events.title: The Battle of Salamis
events.body: A Greek fleet under the Athenian Themistocles lures Xerxes' much larger Persian navy into the narrow straits of Salamis and destroys it, breaking Persia's second invasion of Greece.
events.imageAttribution: Department of History, United States Military Academy, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the Persian advance from Thermopylae to Salamis in 480 BC.

events.title: The Peloponnesian War Begins
events.body: Long-simmering rivalry between Athens and Sparta erupts into open war between their respective alliances, a 27-year conflict that will exhaust both sides and end Athens' golden age.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Captain Blood, translated by Kenmayer, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the alliances and campaigns of the Peloponnesian War.

events.title: Alexander Invades the Persian Empire
events.body: Leading a mostly Macedonian and Greek army across the Hellespont, Alexander wins his first battle against Achaemenid forces at the Granicus River, opening a decade of conquest that will remake the Greek world.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Charles Le Brun, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Charles Le Brun's 1665 painting Le Passage du Granique, depicting Alexander's forces crossing the Granicus River.

events.title: Rome Conquers Greece
events.body: Roman forces defeat the Achaean League at Corinth and raze the city, ending Greek political independence and absorbing the Greek world into Rome's expanding Mediterranean empire.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Tony Robert-Fleury, photographed by Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting depicting the Roman sack of Corinth in 146 BC.

name: Rome
summary: Rome grew from a legendary founding in 753 BC through a Republic that conquered the Mediterranean, into an Empire under Augustus in 27 BC that split its administration under Diocletian in 293 AD -- the Western half finally collapsing in 476 AD while the Eastern half continued for another millennium as the Byzantine Empire.
imageAttribution: Map by Roke, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map tracing Roman territory from the early Republic through the Empire's height and eventual east-west division.

events.title: Legendary Founding of Rome
events.body: Tradition holds that Romulus founds the city of Rome on the Palatine Hill after being raised by a she-wolf; archaeology instead points to a gradual merger of hilltop villages around the same period.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Rabax63, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Capitoline Wolf, a bronze sculpture of a she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, Rome's legendary founders.

events.title: The Roman Republic Is Established
events.body: Rome's last king is overthrown and replaced with elected magistrates and a Senate, beginning nearly five centuries of republican government before power concentrates again under the emperors.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ifly6, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Roman Republic territory in 44 BC, near the end of the Republican era.

events.title: Rome Defeats Hannibal at Zama
events.body: Scipio Africanus decisively defeats Hannibal's Carthaginian army in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War and breaking Carthage as a rival power in the Mediterranean for good.
events.imageAttribution: Sculpture by Sébastien Slodtz, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 18th-century marble sculpture of Hannibal Barca counting the rings taken from Roman knights killed at Cannae.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.body: A group of senators stab Caesar to death in the Theatre of Pompey on the Ides of March, hoping to save the Republic from his growing personal power -- instead triggering the civil wars that end it.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Vincenzo Camuccini, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Vincenzo Camuccini's early 19th-century painting La morte di Cesare (The Death of Caesar), depicting the assassination in the Senate.

events.title: Augustus Becomes Rome's First Emperor
events.body: Octavian, Caesar's adopted heir, takes the title Augustus after defeating his rivals in the civil wars, ending the Republic in all but name and founding the Roman Empire he will rule for over 40 years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Justin Benttinen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Augustus of Prima Porta, a marble statue of Augustus in military dress and one of the best-known portraits of the emperor.

events.title: The Colosseum Opens
events.body: Emperor Titus inaugurates Rome's great amphitheater with a hundred days of games, giving the Empire its most enduring symbol of public spectacle and engineering ambition.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by FeaturedPics, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern photograph of the Colosseum, Rome's great amphitheater, still standing today.

events.title: Diocletian Splits the Empire Into the Tetrarchy
events.body: Facing an empire too vast for one ruler to defend, Diocletian institutes a four-way division of power between two senior and two junior emperors -- an arrangement that foreshadows the later permanent split between East and West.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A late 3rd-century bust of Emperor Diocletian from Nikomedia, modern Izmit, Turkey.

events.title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.body: The Germanic general Odoacer deposes the last Western emperor, the teenage Romulus Augustulus, at Ravenna -- the traditional date marking the end of the Western Roman Empire, while the Eastern half endures as Byzantium.
events.imageAttribution: American Numismatic Society, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A gold solidus coin minted for Romulus Augustulus, the last Western Roman emperor.

name: Persia
summary: Persia was ruled by three successive empires: the Achaemenids, founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC and toppled by Alexander the Great in 330 BC; the Parthians, who threw off Seleucid rule in 247 BC and famously humbled Rome at Carrhae; and the Sasanians, who revived Persian imperial rule in 224 AD and held it until the Arab conquest of 651 AD.
imageAttribution: Map by Cattette, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Achaemenid Empire's territory around 500 BC, near its greatest extent.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Founds the Achaemenid Empire
events.body: Cyrus II defeats the Median Empire and unites the Medes and Persians under Achaemenid rule, founding what will become the largest empire the ancient world had yet seen.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Surenae, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A relief of a winged figure at Pasargadae, Cyrus the Great's capital.

events.title: Cyrus Conquers Babylon, Frees the Jewish Captives
events.body: Cyrus captures Babylon and issues the Cyrus Cylinder, a declaration recording his restoration of displaced peoples and local temples — including freeing the Jewish captives held there since the Babylonian conquest of Jerusalem.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Prioryman, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Cyrus Cylinder, an inscribed clay cylinder recording Cyrus's decrees after taking Babylon, now in the British Museum.

events.title: Construction Begins at Persepolis
events.body: Darius I begins building a new ceremonial capital in the Persian heartland, whose terraces, columned halls, and reliefs will showcase the empire's reach from Egypt to the Indus Valley.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Alborzagros, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Gate of All Nations at Persepolis, the ceremonial entrance to Darius I's palace complex.

events.title: The Battle of Thermopylae
events.body: Xerxes' invading army is delayed for three days at a narrow mountain pass by a small Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas, whose stand becomes a lasting symbol of resistance even in defeat.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Jacques-Louis David, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Jacques-Louis David's 1814 painting Leonidas at Thermopylae, held at the Louvre.

events.title: The Achaemenid Empire Falls to Alexander the Great
events.body: Darius III, the last Achaemenid king, is killed by his own satraps while fleeing Alexander the Great's invasion, bringing the two-century-old empire to an end.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Carole Raddato, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons (detail of the Alexander Mosaic)
events.imageDescription: The Alexander Mosaic, a Roman floor mosaic from Pompeii depicting Alexander the Great's battle against Darius III, now in Naples.

events.title: The Parthian Empire Is Founded
events.body: Arsaces I leads the Parni tribe in seizing the region of Parthia from the crumbling Seleucid Empire, founding a new Iranian dynasty that will rule for the next 470 years.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ro4444 (edited), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Parthian Empire's extent under Mithridates II.

events.title: The Battle of Carrhae
events.body: A Roman invasion force under Crassus is lured into open desert and destroyed by Parthian cavalry under the general Surena, in one of Rome's most catastrophic defeats.
events.imageAttribution: Theodore Ayrault Dodge, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1892 illustration of the Battle of Carrhae from a history of Roman warfare.

events.title: The Sasanian Dynasty Rises
events.body: Ardashir I defeats the last Parthian king and founds a new Persian empire under the House of Sasan, which will rival Rome and later Byzantium for over four centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Ro4444 (edited), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Sasanian Empire's extent under Khosrow II, near its greatest reach.

events.title: Shapur I Captures the Roman Emperor Valerian
events.body: Sasanian king Shapur I defeats a Roman army at Edessa and takes Emperor Valerian prisoner — the first time a reigning Roman emperor is ever captured in battle.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Sasanian rock relief at Naqsh-e Rostam showing Shapur I's triumph over the captured Roman emperor Valerian.

events.title: The Sasanian Empire Falls to Arab Conquest
events.body: After the Rashidun Caliphate's forces overrun the empire, the last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, is murdered while fleeing near Merv, and Persia is absorbed into the expanding Islamic caliphate.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Javierfv1212, edited by HistoryofIran, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Sasanian, Byzantine, and early Muslim territorial borders around the time of the Arab conquest.

name: China
summary: China was unified for the first time by the Qin in 221 BC, and passed through the Han, a long period of division ended by the Sui, the cosmopolitan Tang, and the innovative Song dynasty before the Mongols completed their conquest of the country in 1279 AD.
imageAttribution: Photo by Severin.stalder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling, one of its best-preserved sections.

events.title: Qin Shi Huang Unifies China
events.body: Qin Shi Huang conquers the last rival states and declares himself the first emperor of a unified China, standardizing writing, currency, and law across the new empire.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century portrait of Qin Shi Huang, copied from a 1609 Chinese original.

events.title: Construction Begins on the Great Wall
events.body: Qin Shi Huang orders existing defensive walls linked and extended into a single fortified line across China's northern frontier, the ancestor of the wall that stands today.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Severin.stalder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Wall of China at Jinshanling, part of the fortifications linked under Qin Shi Huang.

events.title: Liu Bang Founds the Han Dynasty
events.body: After defeating his rival Xiang Yu in the Chu-Han Contention, Liu Bang founds the Han dynasty, which will rule China for four centuries and give the Han Chinese their name.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Ming-dynasty portrait of Liu Bang, posthumously honored as Emperor Gaozu, founder of the Han dynasty.

events.title: Cai Lun Refines Papermaking
events.body: Han court official Cai Lun perfects a process for making paper from bark, hemp, and rags, a cheap and practical writing material that will eventually spread across the world.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Cai Lun, the Han court official credited with refining papermaking.

events.title: Sui Wendi Reunifies China
events.body: Emperor Wen ends nearly four centuries of division following the Han collapse, reuniting China under the short-lived Sui dynasty and laying the groundwork for the Grand Canal and the Tang golden age that follows.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Yan Liben, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional Chinese portrait of Emperor Wen of Sui, founder of the short-lived Sui dynasty.

events.title: Tang Taizong Becomes 'Heavenly Khan'
events.body: Emperor Taizong's defeat of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate leads the steppe peoples to acclaim him 'Heavenly Khan,' a title recognizing Tang authority over both China and the nomadic frontier.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of Emperor Taizong of Tang.

events.title: An Lushan Rebellion Devastates Tang China
events.body: General An Lushan revolts against the Tang court, igniting an eight-year civil war so destructive that census records suggest China's population fell by tens of millions -- a blow the dynasty never fully recovers from.
events.imageAttribution: Map by SY, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the territory affected by the An Lushan Rebellion.

events.title: The Song Dynasty Is Founded
events.body: General Zhao Kuangyin is proclaimed emperor by his own troops and founds the Song dynasty, ushering in an era of economic growth, urbanization, and technological innovation like gunpowder and movable-type printing.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A traditional portrait of Song Taizu (Zhao Kuangyin), founder of the Song dynasty, from a scroll later remounted in the Qing dynasty.

events.title: Mongols Conquer the Song Dynasty
events.body: Kublai Khan's fleet destroys the last Song loyalist forces at the naval Battle of Yamen, completing the Mongol conquest of China and founding the Yuan dynasty.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by 长夜无风, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The modern memorial site at Yamen, Guangdong, marking the naval battle that ended the Song dynasty.

name: Maya
summary: The Maya developed one of the ancient world's most sophisticated civilizations across the tropical lowlands of modern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and Honduras, without ever unifying into a single empire. Preclassic cities like Nakbe and El Mirador pioneered monumental pyramid-building by the first millennium BC; the Classic Period (c. 250-900 AD) saw rival city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, and Copán compete through warfare, dynastic marriage, and monumental art before a still-debated collapse depopulated the southern lowlands; and in the Postclassic era power shifted north to Chichen Itza and then Mayapan, whose fall in the 1440s fragmented the Yucatán into small kingdoms that resisted Spanish conquest until the last one fell in 1697.
imageAttribution: Photo by Raymond Ostertag, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: Temple I, the Great Jaguar pyramid, rising over the Great Plaza at Tikal.

events.title: Monumental Construction Begins at Nakbe
events.body: In the Mirador Basin, Nakbe becomes one of the first Maya settlements to raise large stone platforms and pyramids, marking the start of large-scale Maya monumental architecture.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Simon Burchell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A small temple pyramid at Nakbe, one of the earliest major Maya sites.

events.title: El Mirador Rises as the First Great Maya City
events.body: Nearby El Mirador eclipses Nakbe to become the largest Preclassic Maya city, its La Danta pyramid ranking among the largest structures built anywhere in the ancient world by volume.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Konjiki1, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The La Danta pyramid complex at El Mirador, one of the largest structures of the ancient world by volume.

events.title: Preclassic Maya Cities Collapse
events.body: El Mirador and most other major Preclassic centers are abandoned amid drought and political breakdown, closing out the Preclassic period before power later shifts to cities like Tikal.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Authenticmaya, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The jungle-covered Tigre pyramid at El Mirador, abandoned along with the rest of the city by about 150 AD.

events.title: The Classic Period Begins
events.body: Maya city-states like Tikal and Calakmul enter their peak era of monumental architecture, written history, and dynastic rivalry.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Mundo Maya, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Plaza at Tikal, one of the dominant Maya city-states of the Classic Period.

events.title: Teotihuacan's Entrada Remakes Tikal
events.body: A Teotihuacan-backed general, Siyaj K'ak', arrives at Tikal the same day its king dies in battle; within a year a new Teotihuacan-aligned dynasty holds the throne and Tikal's power surges as the distant central Mexican city's proxy in the Maya lowlands.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Greg Willis, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Stela 31 at Tikal, which depicts king Siyaj Chan K'awiil II and records the aftermath of the 378 AD entrada.

events.title: Pakal Ascends the Throne at Palenque
events.body: Twelve-year-old K'inich Janaab' Pakal begins a 68-year reign that will make Palenque one of the Classic Period's greatest artistic centers.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The jade funerary mask and burial regalia of K'inich Janaab' Pakal, displayed at Mexico City's National Museum of Anthropology.

events.title: Quiriguá Captures and Sacrifices Copán's King
events.body: Vassal city Quiriguá defeats its former overlord Copán in battle; king K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat has Copán's ruler Waxaklajuun Ubaah K'awiil beheaded, upending the political order of the southeastern Maya lowlands.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jan Pesula, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Stela E at Quiriguá, a 12-meter monument raised in 771 by K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat, the king who conquered Copán.

events.title: The Last Long Count Date Is Carved
events.body: Monument 101 at Toniná records the final Classic Maya Long Count inscription, as southern lowland cities are abandoned in the following decades.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by J. Antonio Cruz Coutino, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Templo Mayor pyramid at Toniná, the Chiapas hill-city where Maya scribes carved their last Long Count date in 909.

events.title: Chichen Itza Rises to Dominate the Yucatán
events.body: Chichen Itza grows into the peninsula's dominant power, blending Maya and central Mexican Toltec architectural styles at monuments like El Castillo.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Daniel Schwen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: El Castillo, the step pyramid dedicated to Kukulcan at the center of Chichen Itza.

events.title: Mayapan Becomes the Yucatán's New Capital
events.body: Mayapan, a walled city modeled on Chichen Itza, becomes the political and cultural capital of the Yucatán Maya, eventually growing to more than 4,000 structures.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by SiMeCaIS, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ruins of Mayapan, walled capital of the Yucatán Maya from the 1220s to the 1440s.

events.title: Mayapan Collapses, Fragmenting the Yucatán
events.body: Rebellion topples Mayapan's ruling Cocom dynasty, and the Yucatán Maya splinter into rival, often warring city-states with no single dominant capital.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Pavel Vorobiev, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Panoramic view of Mayapan's ruins from the temple of Kukulcan.

events.title: Nojpetén Falls, Ending Independent Maya Rule
events.body: Spanish forces under Martín de Ursúa storm Nojpetén, the Itza capital on Lake Petén Itzá, ending the last independent Maya kingdom more than 175 years after the conquest of Mexico began.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Rafael Amado Deras, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Flores, Guatemala, the modern town built on the island that was once Nojpetén, the Itza Maya capital.

name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The Byzantine Empire carried Roman rule forward in the east for over a thousand years after Constantine founded Constantinople in 330 -- surviving Arab sieges, reaching a medieval peak under Basil II, and enduring the Fourth Crusade's sack of its own capital in 1204 -- before finally falling to the Ottomans in 1453.
imageAttribution: Map by Mnohohrishnyi, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire at the end of Justinian I's reign in 565.

events.title: Constantinople Is Founded
events.body: Emperor Constantine dedicates his new capital on the site of the Greek city of Byzantium, a strategically located city that will anchor Roman power in the east for over a thousand years.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Cplakidas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A topographical map of Constantinople during the Byzantine period.

events.title: Justinian's Code Is Compiled
events.body: Emperor Justinian I orders the compilation of centuries of Roman law into a single authoritative code, a work that will shape legal systems across Europe for centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 13th-century manuscript excerpt of the Code of Justinian with medieval legal commentary in the margins.

events.title: The Hagia Sophia Is Completed
events.body: Justinian I dedicates a vast domed cathedral in Constantinople, an architectural triumph that remains the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Adli Wahid, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A photograph of the Hagia Sophia, the great domed cathedral Justinian I built in Constantinople.

events.title: Greek Fire Repels the Arab Siege of Constantinople
events.body: A year-long Umayyad siege of the Byzantine capital collapses after Byzantine ships destroy the Arab fleet with Greek fire, an incendiary weapon that burns even on water -- a defeat that halts the Islamic conquests' advance into Europe from the east.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Manasses Chronicle, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 14th-century miniature from the Constantine Manasses Chronicle depicting the Arab siege of Constantinople.

events.title: Basil II Crushes Bulgaria at Kleidion
events.body: Byzantine emperor Basil II annihilates the Bulgarian army in a mountain pass, a victory so decisive -- and so brutally followed up -- that it earns him the epithet 'the Bulgar Slayer' and marks the empire's medieval territorial peak.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Manasses Chronicle, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A manuscript illustration showing Basil II's victory over the Bulgarians and the death of Tsar Samuel.

events.title: The Great Schism Divides the Church
events.body: Mutual excommunications between the Pope in Rome and the Patriarch of Constantinople formalize a centuries-old rift, splitting Christianity into Catholic and Orthodox branches that remain divided today.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Barrikader, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of Christianity's eastern and western allegiances following the 1054 schism.

events.title: The Fourth Crusade Sacks Constantinople
events.body: Crusader knights bound for the Holy Land instead storm and pillage Constantinople itself, installing a Latin emperor and shattering Byzantine power so thoroughly that the empire never fully recovers before its final fall two and a half centuries later.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Sailko, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

events.title: Constantinople Falls to the Ottomans
events.body: After a 53-day siege using massive cannon to breach the ancient walls, Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captures Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and the last continuous link to ancient Rome.
events.imageAttribution: Fresco, Moldovița Monastery, photo by DimiTalen, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern fresco at Moldovița Monastery in Romania depicting the siege of Constantinople.

name: Islamic Caliphates
summary: The Islamic Caliphates passed through three successive dynasties: the Rashidun (632-661), whose rapid conquests carried Islam from Arabia across Persia and North Africa; the Umayyads (661-750), ruling from Damascus at their peak from Spain to India; and the Abbasids (750-1258), whose Baghdad-centered Golden Age ended when the Mongols sacked the city in 1258.
imageAttribution: Map by Mohammad adil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Rashidun Caliphate at its greatest territorial extent.

events.title: The Hijra Marks Year One
events.body: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina to escape persecution, an event so pivotal to the Muslim community that it becomes year one of the Islamic calendar.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Islamic miniature depicting the angel Jibril delivering God's instruction for Muhammad to leave Mecca for Medina.

events.title: The Rashidun Caliphate Begins
events.body: Following Muhammad's death, Abu Bakr is chosen as the first caliph, beginning three decades of rapid conquest that will carry Islamic rule from Arabia across Persia, the Levant, and North Africa.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Mohammad adil, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the Rashidun Caliphate's territory at its height, following the conquests begun under Abu Bakr.

events.title: Muawiyah I Founds the Umayyad Caliphate
events.body: After a civil war among Muhammad's early followers, Muawiyah I establishes the Umayyad Caliphate from his power base in Damascus, shifting the seat of Islamic rule from Arabia to Syria and founding a dynasty that will expand from Spain to India.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Arab-Sasanian silver coin of Caliph Muawiyah I, minted in the Umayyad Caliphate's early style.

events.title: The Battle of Tours Halts Umayyad Expansion
events.body: A Frankish army under Charles Martel defeats an Umayyad raiding force deep in what is now France, a battle later mythologized as the moment that stopped the Islamic conquests' advance into Western Europe.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Charles de Steuben, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting of Charles Martel at the Battle of Tours.

events.title: The Abbasid Caliphate Is Founded
events.body: Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah overthrows the Umayyad dynasty and founds the Abbasid Caliphate, which will soon move its capital to the newly built city of Baghdad and preside over an era of scientific and cultural flourishing.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from a Tarikhnama manuscript, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A folio from a Tarikhnama (history) by Balami depicting the proclamation of Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah as the first Abbasid caliph.

events.title: The House of Wisdom Flourishes in Baghdad
events.body: Scholars in Baghdad translate and expand upon Greek, Persian, and Indian texts at a great library and translation center, driving advances in mathematics, astronomy, and medicine during the Islamic Golden Age.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Maqamat al-Hariri manuscript (13th century), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A manuscript illustration of a library, from the Maqamat of al-Hariri.

events.title: Seljuk Turks Take Control of Baghdad
events.body: Sultan Tughril leads Seljuk forces into Baghdad and ends Shia Buyid domination of the Abbasid court, reducing the caliph to a religious figurehead under Sunni Turkic military rule for the remainder of the caliphate's existence.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A miniature depicting the Seljuk sultan Tughril Beg enthroned in Nishapur.

events.title: The Mongols Sack Baghdad
events.body: Hulagu Khan's Mongol army razes Baghdad and executes the last Abbasid caliph, destroying the city's libraries and irrigation works in a catastrophe that ends the Abbasid Caliphate and is remembered as a turning point in the Islamic world's fortunes.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval illustration of the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

name: Khmer Empire
summary: Founded in 802 when Jayavarman II is consecrated as a universal monarch on Phnom Kulen, the Khmer Empire grows into the dominant power of mainland Southeast Asia, centered on the temple-city of Angkor. Its kings build an unmatched sequence of monuments, from Angkor Wat under Suryavarman II to the fortified capital of Angkor Thom and the Bayon under Jayavarman VII, who rebuilds the empire after a Cham fleet sacks the capital in 1177. A Chinese envoy's eyewitness account of Angkor at the turn of the 14th century survives as one of the empire's only outside records, but repeated wars with the rising Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya erode Khmer power until Angkor itself is captured and abandoned in 1431.
imageAttribution: Map by Jembezmamy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of Southeast Asia circa 900 CE, showing the Khmer Empire's territory alongside neighboring Champa and other states.

events.title: Jayavarman II Founds the Khmer Empire
events.body: Atop Mount Mahendraparvata, brahmin priests consecrate Jayavarman II as a chakravartin, or universal monarch, establishing the devaraja cult of divine kingship and unifying rival principalities into the new Khmer Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Xufanc, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Phnom Kulen, the mountain range known in antiquity as Mahendraparvata, where Jayavarman II was consecrated as universal monarch.

events.title: Yasodharapura Becomes the Capital
events.body: King Yasovarman I moves his court to a new capital, Yasodharapura, anchored by the temple-mountain of Phnom Bakheng, dedicated to Shiva on a hill overlooking the site that becomes Angkor.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Satdeep Gill, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Phnom Bakheng, the Shiva temple-mountain at the center of Yasovarman I's new capital, Yasodharapura.

events.title: Construction of Angkor Wat Begins
events.body: Suryavarman II commissions the largest religious monument in the world as his state temple, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Bjørn Christian Tørrissen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Angkor Wat, the front of the main temple complex, photographed in the late afternoon.

events.title: The Cham Sack Angkor
events.body: A Cham fleet under Jaya Indravarman IV sails up the Tonlé Sap, sacks the Khmer capital of Yasodharapura, and kills King Tribhuvanadityavarman, beginning a four-year occupation of the Khmer heartland.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Photo Dharma, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bas-relief at the Bayon temple depicting the Khmer-Cham naval battles fought on the Tonlé Sap.

events.title: Jayavarman VII Expels the Cham and Rebuilds Angkor
events.body: After a four-year campaign to drive out the Cham occupiers, Jayavarman VII is crowned king and launches the empire's largest building program, founding the walled capital of Angkor Thom around the Bayon, his state temple.
events.imageAttribution: Sculpture photographed by Suzan Black, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A sandstone head presumed to depict King Jayavarman VII, in the Bayon style, now in the Musée Guimet, Paris.

events.title: A Chinese Envoy Records Daily Life
events.body: Zhou Daguan, an envoy of the Yuan dynasty, spends nearly a year at Angkor and later writes The Customs of Cambodia, the only detailed eyewitness account of the empire that survives.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Photo Dharma, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A bas-relief at the Bayon depicting a scene of everyday Khmer domestic life, of the kind Zhou Daguan described in his account.

events.title: Ayutthaya Sacks Angkor
events.body: A Siamese army from Ayutthaya captures and loots the Khmer capital after a prolonged siege, prompting King Ponhea Yat to relocate the royal court south toward present-day Phnom Penh.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Supanut Arunoprayote, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Ta Prohm, one of the Angkor temples later reclaimed by jungle after the capital's abandonment.

name: Mongol Empire
summary: Founded in 1206 when a kurultai of steppe chieftains proclaims Temüjin as Genghis Khan, the Mongol Empire grows within two generations into the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled, stretching from the Sea of Japan to the edge of Central Europe. Mongol armies topple the Khwarazmian Empire, the Abbasid Caliphate, and the Song dynasty of China, while cavalry under Batu Khan and Subutai push as far west as Hungary and Poland before a Mamluk army halts their advance at Ain Jalut. A war of succession after Möngke Khan's death splits the empire into four largely independent khanates by the 1260s; the largest, Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty, rules China until Ming rebels drive the Mongols back to the steppe in 1368.
imageAttribution: Map by Wengier (derivative of a map by Teaandcrumpets), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of Asia's political boundaries in 1335, near the Mongol Empire's territorial peak.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongol Tribes
events.body: A kurultai of steppe chieftains gathers at the source of the Onon River and proclaims Temüjin as Genghis Khan, "universal ruler," ending decades of tribal warfare and setting off the fastest territorial expansion in history.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by unknown artist, digitized by the National Palace Museum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A posthumous portrait of Genghis Khan (Taizu), from the Yuan imperial portrait album.

events.title: The Invasion of Khwarazm Begins
events.body: After the governor of Otrar seizes a Mongol trade caravan and executes its merchants, Genghis Khan turns west and invades the Khwarazmian Empire, destroying its great Central Asian cities within two years.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Coopypasted, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An aerial view of the ruins of Otrar, whose governor's seizure of a Mongol caravan triggered the invasion of Khwarazm.

events.title: Mongol Cavalry Crush Hungary at Mohi
events.body: Batu Khan and Subutai's twin invasion of Europe culminates on the Sajó River, where a Mongol army annihilates the royal army of King Béla IV, opening the Hungarian plain to two years of occupation before the Mongols unexpectedly withdraw.
events.imageAttribution: Illumination from the Chronicon Pictum (Cod. 2623), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval illustration from Hayton of Corycus's La Flor des estoires, depicting the Battle of Mohi in 1241.

events.title: The Mongols Sack Baghdad
events.body: Hulagu Khan's army breaches Baghdad's walls, executes the caliph al-Musta'sim, and topples the five-century-old Abbasid Caliphate, extending Mongol power into the heart of the Islamic world.
events.imageAttribution: Painting from Rashid al-Din's Jami al-tawarikh, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A medieval illustration of the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258.

events.title: Mamluks Halt the Mongols at Ain Jalut
events.body: A Mamluk army from Egypt defeats Hulagu's rearguard near the spring of Ain Jalut in Galilee, the first open-field defeat of a Mongol army and the effective limit of the empire's expansion into the Middle East.
events.imageAttribution: Map by MapMaster, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the campaign leading to the 1260 Battle of Ain Jalut.

events.title: The Toluid Civil War Splits the Empire
events.body: Kublai Khan's younger brother Ariq Böke surrenders after a four-year war of succession, but the fighting has already broken the unified Mongol Empire into four largely independent khanates: the Yuan, the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, and the Ilkhanate.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Miskin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 1596 illustration from Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tavarikh depicting Ariq Böke's defeat by Kublai Khan's forces.

events.title: Kublai Khan Founds the Yuan Dynasty
events.body: Genghis Khan's grandson declares a new Chinese dynasty from his capital at Dadu, ruling simultaneously as Great Khan of the Mongols and emperor of China.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by Araniko, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A posthumous portrait of Kublai Khan, painted to make him appear younger than his actual age.

events.title: The Yuan Complete the Conquest of Song China
events.body: A Yuan fleet destroys the last Song loyalist forces at the naval battle of Yamen, ending three centuries of Song rule and bringing all of China under Mongol control for the first time.

events.title: The Yuan Dynasty Falls
events.body: Ming rebels led by Zhu Yuanzhang capture the Yuan capital at Dadu, driving the Mongols back to the steppe and ending nearly a century of Mongol rule over China.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait of the Hongwu Emperor (Zhu Yuanzhang), digitized by the National Palace Museum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A seated portrait of Emperor Ming Taizu (Zhu Yuanzhang), who founded the Ming dynasty after the Yuan's fall.

name: Mali Empire
summary: The Mali Empire rises from the Mandinka heartland along the upper Niger River, founded by Sundiata Keita after his victory at Kirina in 1235. Under Mansa Musa, its ninth ruler, the empire reaches its greatest wealth and territorial extent, and his 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca makes Mali's gold famous across the Islamic world. Timbuktu flourishes as a hub of trade and Islamic scholarship under Mali's patronage, but a long, uneven decline follows Mansa Musa's death: rival Songhai seizes Timbuktu in 1468, and after a catastrophic defeat at Djenné in 1599, the empire fragments for good with the death of its last emperor, Mahmud Keita IV, around 1610.
imageAttribution: Map by HetmanTheResearcher, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map showing the territorial extent of the Mali Empire near its height.

events.title: Sundiata Keita Founds the Mali Empire
events.body: Sundiata Keita leads the united Mandinka clans to victory over the Sosso king Sumanguru Kanté at the Battle of Kirina, is crowned Mansa, and builds the conquered Sosso territories into the new Mali Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Franko Khoury, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 13th- to 15th-century terracotta equestrian figure from Mali, now in the National Museum of African Art.

events.title: Sakura Seizes the Throne and Expands Mali
events.body: Sakura, a former palace dependent from outside the ruling Keita line, seizes power and pushes Mali's borders west to the Atlantic coast and east toward Gao before being killed returning from his own pilgrimage to Mecca around 1300, after which the Keita dynasty is restored.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Franko Khoury, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 13th- to 15th-century terracotta archer figure from Mali.

events.title: Mansa Musa's Pilgrimage to Mecca
events.body: Mali's emperor travels to Mecca with a caravan reportedly carrying tons of gold, spending so freely in Cairo along the way that he depresses the region's gold prices for years afterward.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration attributed to Abraham Cresques, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Mansa Musa enthroned and holding a gold coin, from the 1375 Catalan Atlas.

events.title: Djinguereber Mosque Built in Timbuktu
events.body: Fresh from his pilgrimage, Mansa Musa commissions the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu, part of a wave of building and scholarship that establishes the city as a center of Islamic learning under Mali's patronage.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by KaTeznik, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The courtyard of the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu.

events.title: Songhai Captures Timbuktu
events.body: Sunni Ali's Songhai forces take Timbuktu, which Mali had already lost to Tuareg raiders decades earlier — a milestone in Mali's terminal decline as Songhai rises to become the region's dominant power.
events.imageAttribution: Map by HetmanTheResearcher, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map showing the territorial extent of the Songhai Empire.

events.title: Mali's Defeat at the Battle of Djenné
events.body: Seeking to exploit Songhai's collapse after Morocco's 1591 invasion, Mansa Mahmud Keita IV attacks the trade hub of Djenné but is routed by Moroccan musketeers stationed there, a defeat that shatters what remains of Mali's imperial prestige.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Ondřej Havelka, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Great Mosque of Djenné, in the city where the 1599 battle was fought.

events.title: Mali Empire Ends with the Death of Mahmud Keita IV
events.body: Mali's last reigning emperor, Mahmud Keita IV, dies after retreating to the fortress of Sorokuru; his three sons divide what remains of the realm among themselves, and no single Keita ruler ever governs a unified Mali again.
events.imageAttribution: Diagram by Jansen.2, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A family tree of the Keita dynasty that ruled the Mali Empire.

name: Aztec (Mexica)
summary: Founded in 1325 when the wandering Mexica people build their capital, Tenochtitlan, on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, the Aztec civilization becomes an empire in 1428 when Tenochtitlan joins Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance after defeating the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco. Over the following century Mexica armies and tribute demands extend the alliance's reach across central Mexico, funding a religious capital whose Great Temple is consecrated in 1487 under the ruler Ahuitzotl. Hernán Cortés lands on the Gulf coast in 1519 and, allying with rivals of the Aztecs, marches on Tenochtitlan; after his men are driven out on La Noche Triste in 1520 he returns with a larger force and, aided by a smallpox epidemic that has already killed thousands, besieges and captures the city in 1521, ending Mexica rule.
imageAttribution: Map by Aldan-2, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Aztec Empire's extent in 1519, during the reign of Moctezuma II.

events.title: Tenochtitlan Is Founded
events.body: According to legend, the Mexica see an eagle devouring a serpent atop a cactus — the sign their priests had foretold — and found their capital, Tenochtitlan, on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Roberto Cueva del Río, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 20th-century mural, Fundación de Tenochtitlan, by Roberto Cueva del Río, depicting the city's legendary founding.

events.title: The Triple Alliance Forms
events.body: After the Tepanec usurper Maxtla besieges Tenochtitlan and drives the Acolhua ruler Nezahualcoyotl into exile, the Mexica join Texcoco and the breakaway city of Tlacopan to crush Azcapotzalco, forming the Triple Alliance that becomes the Aztec Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Aztec glyphs for the Triple Alliance's member states by XcepticZP and Goldenbrook, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Aztec glyphs representing the three Triple Alliance city-states: Texcoco, Tenochtitlan, and Tlacopan.

events.title: Axayacatl Conquers Tlatelolco
events.body: Tenochtitlan's tlatoani Axayacatl defeats Moquihuix, ruler of the rival twin city Tlatelolco, in battle and subjects it to Tenochtitlan, bringing the entire island and its great marketplace under unified Mexica rule.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration of Moquihuix from the Codex Mendoza, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of Moquihuix, the defeated ruler of Tlatelolco, from the Codex Mendoza.

events.title: The Great Temple Is Dedicated
events.body: Ruler Ahuitzotl consecrates the rebuilt Templo Mayor on the final day of the month of Panquetzaliztli, its twin shrines to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc marking the Mexica capital near the height of its power.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by GAED, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A photograph of the excavated ruins of the Templo Mayor, Tenochtitlan's Great Temple.

events.title: Moctezuma II Becomes Tlatoani
events.body: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin is crowned as the ninth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, inheriting an empire near its greatest extent that he will rule for nearly two decades before the Spanish arrive.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Codex Durán, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Moctezuma II receiving his crown during his 1502 coronation, illustrated in the 16th-century Codex Durán.

events.title: Cortés Arrives on the Coast
events.body: Hernán Cortés lands on the Gulf coast and founds Veracruz, then marches inland, defeating and then allying with the Tlaxcalans as he advances toward Tenochtitlan.
events.imageAttribution: Portrait by unknown artist (Museo de América collection), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An anonymous portrait of Hernán Cortés, based on a likeness he sent to Paolo Giovio.

events.title: The Spanish Are Driven Out on La Noche Triste
events.body: After Moctezuma II is killed in rioting and Cortés's men loot the palace treasury, the Mexica attack the retreating Spanish column on the causeway out of the city, inflicting heavy losses in what the Spanish call La Noche Triste, the Night of Sorrows.
events.imageAttribution: Anonymous 17th-century painting, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 17th-century oil painting depicting the Spanish retreat from Tenochtitlan under Mexica attack, known as La Noche Triste.

events.title: The Fall of Tenochtitlan
events.body: After a three-month siege and a smallpox epidemic that has already killed thousands, including the previous emperor Cuitláhuac, Spanish forces and their Indigenous allies capture the last tlatoani, Cuauhtémoc, and take Tenochtitlan.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration from the Florentine Codex by Bernardino de Sahagún, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Cortés's brigantine fleet deployed on Lake Texcoco during the siege of Tenochtitlan.

name: Inca
summary: After repelling a Chanka invasion around 1438, Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui rebuilds Cusco into an imperial capital and launches the campaigns that grow the Inca Empire into the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas, stretching along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile and bound together by the Qhapaq Ñan road network. Huayna Capac's death from a mysterious epidemic in 1527 leaves his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fighting a ruinous civil war that Atahualpa wins only months before Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushes and captures him at Cajamarca in 1532. Atahualpa's execution and the Spanish occupation of Cusco end organized imperial rule, but a rump Neo-Inca State holds out in the mountains at Vilcabamba until Spanish forces capture the stronghold and execute its last ruler, Túpac Amaru, in 1572.
imageAttribution: Map by L'Américain, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A modern orthographic map showing the extent of the Inca Empire, Tawantinsuyu, along the Andes.

events.title: Pachacuti Begins the Inca Expansion
events.body: After repelling an invasion by the rival Chanka people, Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui takes the throne, rebuilds Cusco as an imperial capital, and launches the conquests that transform a small highland kingdom into the Inca Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by an unknown artist, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 18th-century portrait of Pachacuti, the ninth Sapa Inca, from a Brooklyn Museum series of paintings of Inca rulers.

events.title: Machu Picchu Is Built
events.body: Pachacuti commissions a royal estate high in the Andes at Machu Picchu, connected to the rest of the empire by the Qhapaq Ñan network of mountain roads and suspension bridges.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Jorge Castro Ruso, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A panoramic view of the Inca citadel of Machu Picchu, built high in the Andes.

events.title: Huayna Capac Dies, Triggering a Succession Crisis
events.body: Emperor Huayna Capac dies at Quito of a mysterious epidemic, possibly a European disease that outran the Spanish themselves, leaving no clear heir and setting his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa on a collision course over the throne.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A period illustration by the Inca chronicler Guaman Poma de Ayala depicting Emperor Huayna Capac.

events.title: Atahualpa Wins the Inca Civil War
events.body: At the Battle of Quipaipan near Cusco, Atahualpa's generals crush Huáscar's army and capture him, ending years of civil war and leaving Atahualpa in control of the empire just as Spanish forces land on the coast.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by John Harris Valda, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A painting depicting the civil war fought between the half-brothers Huáscar and Atahualpa over the Inca throne.

events.title: Atahualpa Is Captured at Cajamarca
events.body: In the town square of Cajamarca, Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force ambushes Atahualpa's unarmed escort, massacring thousands and capturing the emperor, exploiting the recent civil war and the shock of Spanish horses and firearms.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Juan Lepiani, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A painting depicting the capture of Atahualpa by Spanish forces at the Battle of Cajamarca.

events.title: Atahualpa Is Executed
events.body: Despite paying a legendary ransom in gold and silver for his release, Atahualpa is tried and garroted at Cajamarca on charges including treason and the murder of his brother Huáscar, and Spanish forces install a puppet emperor in Cusco.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Luis Montero, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 19th-century painting depicting the funeral of the executed Inca emperor Atahualpa.

events.title: Manco Inca's Rebellion Fails; the Neo-Inca State Is Founded
events.body: Manco Inca Yupanqui, installed by the Spanish as a puppet ruler, turns on his overseers and lays a ten-month siege to Cusco; when it fails, he retreats to the remote mountain refuge of Vilcabamba and founds the independent Neo-Inca State.
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A period illustration by the Inca chronicler Guaman Poma de Ayala depicting Manco Inca's uprising against Spanish rule.

events.title: The Last Inca Stronghold Falls
events.body: Spanish forces capture Túpac Amaru in the forests west of Vilcabamba, march him to Cusco, and publicly behead him before thousands in the central square, ending organized Inca resistance four decades after Pizarro's first landing.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by an unidentified Cuzco School painter, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A Cuzco School portrait of Túpac Amaru, the last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State.

name: Japan
summary: The Yamato clan's chieftains unify much of Japan from the Nara Basin around 300 AD, and over the next millennium the country moves through waves of continental influence -- Buddhism, Chinese-style law codes, and courtly aristocracy -- before military governments led by shoguns take real power from 1192 onward. Centuries of feudal warfare give way to Tokugawa unification and two and a half centuries of enforced isolation, which ends when American warships force Japan open in 1853 and the shogunate collapses in the 1868 Meiji Restoration.
imageAttribution: Photo by 663highland, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: The Great Buddha Hall of Tōdai-ji temple in Nara, one of Japan's most significant early Buddhist temples.

events.title: Yamato Polity Unifies the Nara Basin
events.body: Chieftains of the Yamato clan consolidate power over the Nara Basin and neighboring regions, founding the imperial line that rules Japan, at least in name, to the present day.
events.imageAttribution: Map by Immanuelle, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of ethnic groups within the early Yamato polity.

events.title: Buddhism Arrives from Baekje
events.body: King Seong of the Korean kingdom of Baekje sends Emperor Kinmei's court a Buddha image, sutras, and ritual banners, introducing Buddhism to Japan and beginning its long fusion with native Shinto practice.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Chris 73, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Asuka Great Buddha at Asuka-dera, Japan's oldest Buddhist temple, founded soon after Buddhism's introduction.

events.title: Isshi Incident Triggers the Taika Reform
events.body: Prince Naka no Ōe and Nakatomi no Kamatari assassinate the powerful minister Soga no Iruka at court, clearing the way for Emperor Kōtoku's Taika Reform, which recasts Japan's government along centralized Chinese Tang lines.
events.imageAttribution: Scroll painting by Gukei Sumiyoshi, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A depiction of the assassination of Soga no Iruka from the Tōnomine Engi scroll, painted in the Edo period.

events.title: Capital Moves to Heian-kyō
events.body: Emperor Kanmu relocates the capital to Heian-kyō, opening the four-century Heian period in which a hereditary court aristocracy presides over a golden age of Japanese literature and art.
events.imageAttribution: Illustrated scroll from The Tale of Genji, Imperial court in Kyoto, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A scene from the illustrated Tale of Genji handscroll (Genji Monogatari Emaki), an early 12th-century work depicting Heian court life.

events.title: Minamoto no Yoritomo Becomes Shogun
events.body: Minamoto no Yoritomo receives the title of shogun from the emperor, formalizing the military government he had already built at Kamakura and beginning nearly seven centuries of rule by warrior-class shoguns rather than the imperial court.
events.imageAttribution: Woodblock print by Utagawa Sadahide, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1862 print depicting Minamoto no Yoritomo's procession into Kyoto, around 1190.

events.title: Kamikaze Repel the Second Mongol Invasion
events.body: A typhoon destroys Kublai Khan's invasion fleet off Kyushu for the second time in seven years, ending Mongol attempts to conquer Japan and giving rise to the legend of the kamikaze, or "divine wind."
events.imageAttribution: Illustration by Qiushufang, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A map of the two Mongol invasion routes into Japan in 1274 and 1281.

events.title: Ōnin War Shatters Central Authority
events.body: A succession dispute among the shogunate's leading families erupts into a decade of fighting centered on Kyoto, permanently weakening the Ashikaga shogunate and opening the Sengoku, or "Warring States," era of rival regional daimyo.
events.imageAttribution: Woodblock print by Utagawa Yoshitora, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: The Battle of Ōnin during the Ōnin War (1467-1477), depicted by Utagawa Yoshitora.

events.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu Wins at Sekigahara
events.body: Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern Army crushes the rival Western coalition at Sekigahara, a victory that ends over a century of civil war and, three years later, brings him the title of shogun, founding the Tokugawa shogunate that rules Japan for the next two and a half centuries.
events.imageAttribution: Folding screen painting, Collection of the Town of Sekigahara Archive of History and Cultural Anthropology, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A folding screen (byōbu) depicting the Battle of Sekigahara, based on an early 17th-century original.

events.title: Commodore Perry Forces Japan Open
events.body: US Commodore Matthew Perry sails a squadron of warships into Uraga, forcing the Tokugawa shogunate to abandon over two centuries of sakoku isolation and open Japanese ports to American trade.
events.imageAttribution: Japanese print, artist unknown, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An 1854 Japanese print of Commodore Perry's fleet, showing one of the two paddlewheel steamers on his visit.

events.title: Meiji Restoration Ends the Shogunate
events.body: Emperor Meiji is restored to direct political power and the last shogun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, surrenders his authority, ending nearly 700 years of shogunate rule and launching Japan's rapid modernization.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Takahashi Yuichi, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Emperor Meiji by Takahashi Yuichi, held in the Imperial Collection.

name: Ottoman Empire
summary: The Ottoman Empire grows from a small Turkoman frontier principality founded by Osman I around 1299 into a vast Islamic empire spanning Europe, Asia, and North Africa -- conquering Constantinople in 1453, reaching its height under Suleiman the Magnificent, and surviving repeated wars and reform efforts before the Grand National Assembly abolishes the sultanate in 1922.
imageAttribution: Map by Chamboz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
imageDescription: A map of the Ottoman Empire's territorial extent in 1683, near its greatest reach.

events.title: Osman I Founds the Ottoman Beylik
events.body: Osman I, a Turkoman frontier lord ruling from the small Anatolian town of Söğüt, breaks from Seljuk overlordship and founds the beylik that will grow into the Ottoman Empire.
events.imageAttribution: Ottoman miniature painting, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: An Ottoman miniature portrait of Osman I, founder of the Ottoman Empire.

events.title: Mehmed II Conquers Constantinople
events.body: Sultan Mehmed II breaches Constantinople's ancient walls after a 53-day siege using massive cannon, ending the Byzantine Empire and transforming Ottoman rule from a regional power into an empire straddling Europe and Asia.
events.imageAttribution: Fresco, Moldovita Monastery, photo by DimiTalen, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A modern fresco at Moldovita Monastery in Romania depicting the siege of Constantinople.

events.title: Suleiman the Magnificent Besieges Vienna
events.body: Suleiman the Magnificent lays siege to the Habsburg capital of Vienna but withdraws after 18 days when rain, dwindling supplies, and the approaching winter make the walls unbreakable in time -- marking the deepest advance of Ottoman power into Central Europe.
events.imageAttribution: Engraving by Bartel Beham, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A contemporary engraving depicting the 1529 Ottoman siege of Vienna.

events.title: The Holy League Destroys the Ottoman Fleet at Lepanto
events.body: A Holy League fleet of Spanish, Venetian, and papal galleys crushes the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Patras, ending decades of unchallenged Ottoman dominance at sea even as the empire rebuilds its fleet within a year.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by Laureys a Castro, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A 17th-century painting depicting the naval Battle of Lepanto.

events.title: The Ottomans Are Routed at the Battle of Vienna
events.body: A relief army led by Polish king John III Sobieski smashes the two-month Ottoman siege of Vienna, halting the empire's westward expansion for good and touching off a sixteen-year war that steadily rolls back Ottoman territory in Europe.
events.imageAttribution: Painting, Museum of Military History Vienna, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A monumental painting depicting the 1683 siege and relief of Vienna.

events.title: The Treaty of Karlowitz Ends the Great Turkish War
events.body: Defeated in the Great Turkish War, the Ottoman Empire signs the Treaty of Karlowitz, ceding Hungary and other territories to the Habsburgs, Podolia to Poland-Lithuania, and Dalmatia and the Morea to Venice in its first major territorial retreat from a coalition of European powers.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by O.Mustafin, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A copy of the Treaty of Karlowitz document exhibited in the Doge's Palace in Venice.

events.title: The Edict of Gülhane Launches the Tanzimat Reforms
events.body: Sultan Abdülmecid I proclaims the Edict of Gülhane at Topkapı Palace, launching the Tanzimat era of reforms that overhaul Ottoman law, education, and taxation in an attempt to modernize the empire and halt its long decline.
events.imageAttribution: Painting by David Wilkie, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: A portrait of Sultan Abdülmecid I, who proclaimed the Edict of Gülhane.

events.title: The Young Turk Revolution Restores the Constitution
events.body: Army officers of the Committee of Union and Progress rise up in Ottoman Macedonia and force Sultan Abdul Hamid II to restore the suspended 1876 constitution, ending three decades of autocratic rule and opening the empire's final constitutional era.
events.imageAttribution: Photo by Charles Roden Buxton, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Religious leaders of different faiths appearing together to mark the 1908 constitutional restoration.

events.title: The Grand National Assembly Abolishes the Sultanate
events.body: The Grand National Assembly in Ankara abolishes the Ottoman sultanate, stripping Sultan Mehmed VI of political power and formally ending over six centuries of Ottoman rule as the last sultan departs Constantinople into exile.
events.imageAttribution: Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
events.imageDescription: Sultan Mehmed VI departing Dolmabahçe Palace shortly before his exile in November 1922.

name: Vikings (Norse)
